title: Greed is a dog
hookLine: greed is a dog, falsehood a scavenger, cheating is eating carrion (Sri Rag M1, ang 15)

cards: There's a dog in every neighborhood that knows exactly when the trash goes out. It was fed an hour ago and still stands at the gate, nose working, eyes on the bag. Not because it's hungry.
Because it's a dog. Some of us have met a version of that dog inside: at a buffet, in a sale, scrolling past one more thing nobody needs.
One page after the dream house, Guru Nanak names that dog out loud, and he doesn't soften it.

teach.b: The shabad is in Sri Rag, on ang 15. Its first lines run, in effect: greed is a dog; falsehood is a scavenger; cheating is eating carrion. Slandering others is putting their filth in your own mouth.
Anger is a fire that burns like an outcast's pyre. Then the punch: these tastes and this self-praise, these are my deeds, O Creator. The word for greed is lab, the hungry wanting that's never full.
Two things to notice. First, the language is harsh on purpose.
Guru Nanak takes the insults of his day, the names a caste society threw at people it looked down on, and throws them at the vices instead. It's the greed that's the dog, the lying that's unclean.

The Gurus rejected caste outright, and here the shock of those words is turned around: the real lowness isn't in anyone's birth. It's in what a person does. Second, the surprise: the shabad is in the first person.

Not you are greedy, not they are liars, but these are my deeds. The Guru speaks the confession himself, so anyone singing it says it about themselves, and nobody gets to point at the person across the hall.

teach.h: SPEAK IN A WAY THAT BRINGS HONOR.
teach.b: The refrain then turns to speech: speak in a way that brings honor; those whose deeds are good are called good at the Lord's door.
So the dog isn't destiny. A dog can be noticed. It can be trained, or at least told no.
The first step is just seeing it at the gate.

how: Sikhs sing this Sri Rag shabad of Guru Nanak in kirtan; its first-person confession, these are my deeds, is sung by the whole congregation about themselves.

o: anger, a fire that burns inside
greed, the hungry wanting never full

games.q: greed is a dog — tap the pairs.
p: others' filth in your own mouth

s: the hymn is aimed at other people's sins
it's in the first person: these are my deeds, O Creator.
the shabad turns insults of a caste society against the vices
the lowness is in what a person does, not in anyone's birth.
the refrain says the good are called good at the Lord's door
speak in a way that brings honor.

games.q: you're writing a hymn about greed, lying and anger. who do you say is guilty?
games.why: Guru Nanak confesses in the first person, so everyone who sings it confesses with him.

practice: Think back over today or yesterday and find one moment when you wanted more than you needed: one more helping, one more purchase, one more scroll.

Don't scold yourself; just see it, the way you'd see a dog at the gate, and notice where you felt it in your body. Breathe, and let it sit there without obeying it; if you pray, you can say Waheguru to it, quietly.

wordCard.voice: Lab, the hungry wanting that's never full: Guru Nanak names it, lying, cheating and slander, and confesses them as his own deeds, so everyone who sings it does the same.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: greed, a dog; the opening words of the shabad.

carryVoice: Your line: mind the dog. Seen at the gate, it doesn't have to be fed. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sri Rag M1, Ang 15 (lab kutaa koorh choohraa)
